name: Pediatric lateral-trochanteric entry for rigid femoral nailing
corridor: Longitudinal lateral fascia-lata split to a start lateral and inferior to the greater-trochanter tip, collinear with the canal on the lateral view

positioning.text: Position supine on a radiolucent table with the proximal lateral femur accessible and the entire femur imageable in AP and lateral planes.

setup.text: Confirm skeletal maturity, trochanteric anatomy, canal size, fracture reduction strategy, and compatibility of the implant with a lateral entry before incision.

surface_landmarks.text: Mark the palpable greater-trochanter tip, anterior and posterior trochanter borders, femoral axis, and a lateral fluoroscopic projection of the canal.

incision.text: Center the incision on the trochanter tip, extending about 3 cm proximally and distally as required, in line with the medullary canal on the lateral image.

superficial_interval.text: Incise fascia lata longitudinally in the same direction and spread the underlying tissues to expose the lateral greater trochanter.

deep_interval.text: Palpate both trochanter borders and establish the nail entry lateral and inferior to the greater-trochanter tip under orthogonal fluoroscopy.

layers.text: Skin, subcutaneous tissue, fascia lata, limited abductor-vastus soft-tissue corridor, trochanteric cortex, then femoral canal.

structures_encountered.text: Fascia lata, greater trochanter, abductor insertion region, proximal femoral cortex, and medullary canal define the approach.

structures_at_risk.text: The greater-trochanteric apophysis, abductor mechanism, proximal femoral cortex, femoral-neck blood supply, and posterior cortex are at risk from an incorrect portal or trajectory.

danger_zones.text: Avoid a piriformis-fossa portal in a skeletally immature patient and avoid medial, superior, anterior, or posterior deviation from the implant-specific lateral start.

retraction_hazards.text: Do not lever instruments against the trochanter or abductors to compensate for a poorly aligned incision; extend the skin and fascia until the working path is collinear.

exposure.text: Provides a physeal-conscious lateral portal for a compatible locked rigid nail without opening the shaft fracture.

limitations.text: Requires an adequately sized canal and a patient and fracture pattern appropriate for locked nailing; it is not interchangeable with piriformis-entry implant geometry.

extensions.text: Extend proximally or distally along the lateral incision to obtain a collinear track; use a separate limited reduction window only when closed reduction fails.

indications.text: Use in selected older, heavier children or adolescents with femoral-shaft fractures unsuitable for flexible nails and suitable for a lateral-entry locked nail.

relative_contraindications.text: Avoid when patient size, open proximal femoral growth anatomy, canal diameter, fracture location, infection, or implant design prevents a safe lateral-entry construct.

implant_implications.text: Use only a nail designed for pediatric lateral-trochanteric entry; match diameter and curvature to the canal and keep guidewire, reamer, and nail on the planned axis.

fluoroscopy_implications.text: Confirm the portal lateral and inferior to the trochanter tip on AP view and collinear with the canal laterally, then monitor reduction, reaming, depth, and locking across the whole femur.

closure.text: Irrigate, obtain hemostasis, repair fascia lata without abductor tethering, and close subcutaneous tissue and skin.

complications.text: Complications include growth disturbance, abductor injury, osteonecrosis, trochanteric or neck fracture, cortical perforation, malalignment, nonunion, infection, and hardware irritation.

bailouts.text: If the implant-specific safe start cannot be achieved, stop repeated opening attempts and change positioning, exposure, or fixation strategy rather than using a hazardous portal.

procedure_applications.condition: An older or heavier pediatric patient is selected for a pediatric lateral-entry locked nail, with sufficient canal size and open-growth-plate considerations addressed

questions.question: Where is the rigid lateral-entry start?
questions.answer: On the lateral greater trochanter, lateral and inferior to its tip.

questions.question: How is the incision aligned?
questions.answer: With the medullary canal on the lateral fluoroscopic view.

questions.question: Why avoid piriformis entry in an immature patient?
questions.answer: It risks proximal femoral blood supply and growth-related complications; a compatible lateral-entry design is preferred.
